tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file outside the working directory, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not.
- Prefer the Edit tool for modifying existing files — it only sends the diff. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- NEVER create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

tools.name: SubagentHandback
tools.description:
Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}) as your last tool call and then stop. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

Only a report delivered through SubagentHandback reaches your caller; plain text you write at the end of your turn is NOT delivered. There is no recipient parameter: the report can only go to your caller.

Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

## zotero-research
Read-only access to the user's Zotero research library. For substantive sport-science questions, build a Zotero-first evidence pack before answering. Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. SecondBrain Queue is the priority lane; promotion eligibility is controlled by promotion_scope.

| File | Round-2 status | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `_book.md` | FIX (new error) | The reconciliation of Eric's "lost the table" remark is correct: Part-3.pdf p.2 does list the Level 1-5 bands. New error: "Part-3.pdf p.3 states a single floor of >=1.8x". The PDF p.3 text is "Seated calf isometric benchmarks (e.g., 1.8× bodyweight peak force)". It has no "≥" and no floor wording. 19	3. **Force production benchmarks** in the injured area, e.g. eccentric hamstring strength via Nordic at roughly 80-85% of pre-injury baseline; seated calf isometric peak force. The same page gives the range framing for the hamstring number (80-85%). Use 1.7-1.8x as the working range for the calf figure and confirm against the athlete's own baseline.
20	4. **Reactive strength/stretch-shortening-cycle function**, e.g. via a hopping task, to check the athlete can produce high force in a short timeframe before near-maximal speed.
21	
22	The transcript checker, not Harries, marks an injury term near ~15:51 as unclear (`[injury term unclear] strain` in the source transcript); it has been left unresolved rather than guessed.
23	
24	**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: "there are of course varied opinions in the field on this criteria, especially in regard to the assessment of force production capacities... it seems sensible to me and has almost zero downside" (~15:21-15:36). Eric's review classifies these as expert opinion, not trial results; Harries himself only says "varied opinions in the field," not that framing. Label them that way whenever they are used, and do not present the 80-85%, 1.7-1.8x, or hop-test criteria as validated thresholds.
25

14	# Case Study: Semimembranosus Strain With Adductor Magnus Involvement (Case 2)
15	
16	**What it is** — Grade 2 strain, classified as "`[classification name unclear]` 2B, proximal hamstring strain with a longitudinal tendon split" (the classification system name is unclear in the audio near ~02:24 and is left unresolved here), acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. RTP day 30: six rehab-running sessions, two modified-training sessions, three full-training sessions. **The athlete returned to play one week earlier than the medical/performance team's own recommendation** - Harries flags this explicitly as "the real world nature of decision making" (~02:36-02:46).
17	
18	**Max velocity progression.** Days 0-4 off legs; two non-consecutive running exposures week 1 (days 5, 7); three non-consecutive sessions week 2, increasing intensity/volume. Sessions 1-5: linear increase (mechanics drills, time-based 100 m repeats, then faster 60 m repeats, then strides, then flies). Sessions 6-8: undulating pattern. **Two exposures above 90% MV were achieved before return**: day 22 at 96.7% and day 27 at 92.1% - Harries calls this "a strong application of progressive loading." Session 5 is stated to be functionally identical to Case 1's session 5 (60 m reps building 18-22.5 km/h, then six strides: two at 70-75%, two at 75-80%, two at ~82.5% MV, effort-based and GPS-confirmed), which he says typifies a mid-rehab max-velocity checkpoint around day 10-14 post-injury, with ~85% MV treated as a sound ceiling until force-production and reactive-strength criteria are confirmed and there has been adequate time for biological healing (~21:00). Session 8 (coinciding with return to full training): progressive 60 m strides, three 20 m flies at 85-95% MV, and **repeat sprint intervals**: two sets of three to four reps over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s) - see [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]].
19	
20	**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Same thresholds as Case 1 (17/23/27 km/h). Session 2 produced an unexpected HSR overshoot via 100 m repeats; Harries notes this matters less here because 17 km/h is only ~55-60% of max for these athletes (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]). From session 3, HSR delivered via short-interval formats (10 s on/10 s off, 20 s on/20 s off); from session 8, small-sided games contributed HSR organically. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 4-8, but **session 7/day 19 under-dosed at only 40% of game volume** (Harries wanted 70-80%); session 8 then peaked at 120% of game value.
21	
22	**MDSA.** Sessions 2-3: basic curvilinear runs, linear/lateral shuffling. Session 4: low-velocity cutting, basic accel/decel drills. Sessions 5-6: velocity change graded up, closed reactivity (visual/verbal cues) added. Session 7: higher entry/change velocities, larger spaces, still closed-reactive. Session 8: evasive drills at lower velocities in smaller spaces (deliberately lower isolated-MDSA volume that session, offset by a fortunate scheduling window - the reserves team's bye gave more athletes for higher-quality skill-drill exposure instead). Session 9 onward: high-velocity evasive MDSA in realistic/competitive contexts.
23	
24	**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 2-3: low-load stationary handball/short kicking. Sessions 3-4: controlled movement added to technical execution. Sessions 5-6: positional-specific drills with movement fatigue. Sessions 7-8: small-group competitive play (3v3, 5v5 handball). Week 4: large-group competitive play in the main training session before return.
25	
26	**Why it works** — This case shows the framework producing a well-dosed sprint exposure (two exposures >90% MV, repeat-sprint intervals for fatigue-state sprinting) even while the actual return date was moved up by organizational decision-making outside the physical-readiness plan.
27	
28	**When to apply** — Use as the reference case for "physical readiness criteria met or exceeded, but the actual return decision still overridden by other factors" - a reminder that meeting the framework's numbers does not by itself control the return-to-play date.
29	
30	**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported; the one-week-early return is presented as a fact of what happened, not validated as safe by any outcome data beyond it being reported without a stated recurrence.
31	
32	**Example** — See [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]] for the reusable session-design pattern this case's session 8 exemplifies.
33	
34	**Related** — [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]
35

15	
16	**What it is** — In the back half of late-rehab sessions, Harries introduces repeat-sprint intervals to expose the athlete to high velocity under fatigue and simulate conditioning demand alongside sprint load. The format, used across three of the four case studies: **1-2 sets of three to four repetitions over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start** (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s, etc.). Case 2 used **two sets**; Cases 3 and 4 used **one set** (~21:23-21:59, ~30:49-30:58, ~40:14-40:23).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: placing these in the back half of the session, after other running/skill work has already introduced some fatigue, "blends" high-speed exposure with a controlled recovery interval, giving both a sprint-load-accumulation stimulus and a conditioning stimulus at once. Inference (entry writer's, not stated by Harries): this rehearses producing near-maximal velocity in a fatigued state closer to what a game actually demands late in a match.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Use in the return-to-sport-phase session(s), once an athlete has already cleared the 75-85% MV gate and is accumulating >90% MV exposures elsewhere in the session (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). # Repeat-Sprint Interval Format for Late-Stage Fatigue Exposure

**What it is** — In the back half of late-rehab sessions, Harries introduces repeat-sprint intervals to expose the athlete to high velocity under fatigue and simulate conditioning demand alongside sprint load. The format, used across three of the four case studies: **1-2 sets of three to four repetitions over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start** (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s, etc.). Case 2 used **two sets**; Cases 3 and 4 used **one set** (~21:23-21:59, ~30:49-30:58, ~40:14-40:23).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: placing these in the back half of the session, after other running/skill work has already introduced some fatigue, "blends" high-speed exposure with a controlled recovery interval, giving both a sprint-load-accumulation stimulus and a conditioning stimulus at once. Inference (entry writer's, not stated by Harries): this rehearses producing near-maximal velocity in a fatigued state closer to what a game actually demands late in a match.

**When to apply** — Use in the return-to-sport-phase session(s), once an athlete has already cleared the 75-85% MV gate and is accumulating >90% MV exposures elsewhere in the session (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). Inference: scale the number of sets (one vs two) to the athlete's overall session load and injury type - the lower-frequency recurrent-calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) used only one set, though Harries does not state this as a rule.

**When NOT to apply** — This is placed deliberately late in rehab, after force-production benchmarks are already cleared; it should not be used as an early-rehab or pre-gate exposure, since it combines near-maximal velocity with accumulated fatigue, precisely the combination the earlier gate criteria are designed to screen for readiness against.

**Example** — See [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 8 for the two-set version and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 10 for the one-set version used alongside a knee-joint injury.

**Related** — [[framework--broken-stride-timing-protocol]]

lines: **What it is** — Weber's model of the full route from an observation to an action: **data capture -> quality control -> analysis -> interpretation -> communication -> decision and action** (Video Lab 6D summary, 00:00–02:02). He names a specific gap between each pair of adjacent stages. **(1) Dirty data** (capture to quality control): check that the collection protocol was actually followed and that anomalies are caught before entering reports or a long-term database, with a named owner for the check. **(2) Expertise** (quality control to analysis): a reliable measurement can still be judged against an unsuitable threshold, or without its normal context, including software defaults that were never reviewed. **(3) Interpretation** (analysis to meaning): a number can reach a meeting with no one stating what it means for the athlete or the decision, and excess data can exceed the team's capacity to interpret it. **(4) Communication** (interpretation to decision-maker): technical language can obscure the actual requested action; Weber recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. **(5) Authority** (recommendation to action): even a clear recommendation can be ignored without a formal decision gate or override process; he calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions (02:02–10:50).

-**Why it works** — **Inference:** naming a specific gap between each pair of stages turns a vague complaint (data that does not seem to change anything) into a locatable failure point, the same diagnostic logic as [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] but applied at the level of a single decision's data pipeline rather than the department's overall structure. Weber himself does not state this general mechanism, only the six-stage model and its five gaps.

+**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: pathways break "not because the people are bad at jobs, but the process has a gap. Steps are not defined and people's roles within those steps are not defined" (6D transcript 00:00:42 to 00:00:52), and naming the stages lets a team "name exactly where your pathway is breaking" (00:00:57 to 00:01:06). Inference: this is the same diagnostic logic as [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]], applied to a single decision's pipeline.

**When to apply** — Weber's own stated practical use: trace a recent important decision through all six stages, identify the gap that most affects decisions, and assign a concrete owner and process to close it (10:52–12:11). **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, with no sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently documented [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment; Load monitoring and GPS]. **Inference:** Weber's expertise-gap point, that someone needs to set and review the thresholds a measurement is judged against, including software defaults, lands directly on that named gap; this framework gives it a specific owner-and-process fix rather than leaving it as a general observation.
# The Integration Problem: Five Break Points Between Data and Decision

-**What it is** — Weber's framework for a specific failure mode: a practitioner collects genuinely useful information, but it never influences a decision because the organization has no reliable way to interpret, discuss, or act on it. "Good information does not guarantee influence... this is usually not a knowledge problem" (The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet.pdf p.1). His five break points, tracing a signal from collection to action: **(1) language gap** — teams use different terms or underlying models for athlete status, readiness, risk, or rehabilitation; **(2) decision pathway gap** — no agreed route identifies who collects, reviews, discusses, and uses technical information, or what triggers a conversation; **(3) authority gap** — a senior decision-maker can override a technical recommendation without discussion or explanation (Weber favors hearing competing cases and explaining the decision, rather than a silent override); **(4) relationship deficit** — the person who must act does not yet understand or trust the evidence; per the lesson summary, Weber frames this as a shared responsibility, with practitioners sharing responsibility for preparing colleagues to interpret new information; **(5) process absence** — missing meeting gates, decision checkpoints, or review steps let a team skip important intermediate judgments (Video Lab 6A summary, 06:58–13:14; cheat sheet p.1). His diagnostic test: "if your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak" (cheat sheet p.1).

+**What it is** — Weber's framework for a specific failure mode: a practitioner collects genuinely useful information, but it never influences a decision because the organization has no reliable way to interpret, discuss, or act on it. "Good information does not guarantee influence... this is usually not a knowledge problem" (The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet.pdf p.1). His five break points, tracing a signal from collection to action: **(1) language gap** — teams use different terms or underlying models for athlete status, readiness, risk, or rehabilitation; **(2) decision pathway gap** — no agreed route identifies who collects, reviews, discusses, and uses technical information, or what triggers a conversation; **(3) authority gradient** — a senior decision-maker can override a technical recommendation without discussion or explanation (Weber favors hearing competing cases and explaining the decision, rather than a silent override); **(4) relationship deficit** — the person who must act does not yet understand or trust the evidence; per the lesson summary, Weber frames this as a shared responsibility, with practitioners sharing responsibility for preparing colleagues to interpret new information; **(5) process absence** — missing meeting gates, decision checkpoints, or review steps let a team skip important intermediate judgments (Video Lab 6A summary, 06:58–13:14; cheat sheet p.1). His diagnostic test: "if your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak" (cheat sheet p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's core claim, stated directly, is that departments fail through structure, not intent: recommendations get ignored, diluted, or misunderstood because the environment lacks the pathway to handle them, not because the underlying analysis was wrong (cheat sheet p.1). **Inference:** naming five distinct break points turns a vague sense that good work isn't landing into a specific, auditable question, which of the five links actually failed.

There is no control, and the selection is plainly of successes. The hurdler also had a new collaborating coach, "great coaching and great technical training," per Natera himself. Elsewhere (~34:19–35:15) he reports programs where RSI was "the only change," and he concedes that is "not exactly a controlled scientific experiment." # HSR/VHSR Delivery Shifts: Structured Repeats, Then Short Intervals, Then Small-Sided Games

**What it is** — Across the case studies, high-speed running (HSR/VHSR) volume is not just dosed up session to session, it is delivered through three successive formats as rehab advances. Early sessions accumulate HSR through structured, individually-prescribed repeats over a fixed distance (e.g. 100 m and 60 m repeats). # Fitting Rehab Sessions Into the Team's Own Training Week

**What it is** — As a returning athlete moves from an isolated running-only schedule into overlapping with team training, Harries shapes each week of rehab around the team's own weekly training rhythm, not a fixed rehab-only calendar. Case 1, week 3: "a high moderate high structure, including partial training exposure in the midweek, and a heavier modified training session on the weekend" (~05:18-05:27). Case 1, week 4: "one light partial session, a full training midweek, and a walkthrough style session... And then they played their game at the end of the week" (~05:27-05:37). Case 2, week 3: a small on-field rehab session early in the week, a return to partial training midweek, then "a larger combined rehab session with modified team training" at week's end (~17:44-17:56). Case 2, week 4: two non-consecutive training days then two consecutive days, the second-to-last being "a captain's run walkthrough style session, though very low intensity," followed by return to play in a match (~17:56-18:10). Case 4 (knee), week 5: running frequency was deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions "in order to make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions," explicitly to bridge into the larger session planned at the end of week 6 (~37:24-37:46). Case 4, week 7 (the RTP week): "a small session early in the week, a moderate session mid-week, which was aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season," then return to play at week's end (~38:13-38:26).

**Why it works** — For the Case 4 frequency cut, Harries states the reason directly: reducing running frequency let him "make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions" so there was "a nice little progression into" the larger, match-comparable session planned for the following week (~37:26-37:55). For the broader practice of shaping rehab-week structure around the team's rhythm, his only stated reason is the week-7 mid-week session "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (~38:20-38:22); he gives no further explicit rationale for the general practice. Inference (entry writer's): tying rehab-session load to the team's own hard/light day pattern lets the returning athlete's tolerance build in step with what full training will actually demand in the week he returns, rather than on a schedule disconnected from it.

**When to apply** — When designing a returning athlete's week once he is off an isolated running-only schedule and beginning to overlap with team sessions (typically mid-to-late rehab, alongside modified/partial training participation). Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records an existing preference for undulating, not linear, weekly periodization ("waving volume week to week"), and an explicit note that a "training week" does not have to equal 7 calendar days but should be built around the team's real competition schedule; this on-field-rehab pattern applies that same logic to one returning athlete inside the team's actual week.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed template; no claim is made that a "high-moderate-high" week or a captain's-run walkthrough is required, and the specific weekly shapes differ across all three cases that show them, tracking each athlete's own timeline and injury type. None of it is validated against outcome data beyond what happened in each case being reported without a stated recurrence. Do not import a specific case's weekly pattern wholesale as a template; use the underlying idea, build the rehab week around the team's actual week, and rebuild the specific days for each returning athlete.

**Example** — See [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]], weeks 5-7, for the clearest stated rationale: a frequency cut used as a deliberate bridge to a larger session, and an RTP week deliberately matched to the team's normal in-season training rhythm.

He adds that the session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding" (~20:08-20:14).

# The Five-Element Case-Review Structure

**What it is** — Harries reviews each of his four case studies through the same five elements, stated explicitly: "the rehab timeline, which is a high-level overview of the return to play calendar"; "the loading structure. So how was loading planned and how was it progressed across on-field rehab"; "the progression of maximum velocity and how those linear running intensities were increased"; "our multi-directional speed and agility progressions and how we developed acceleration, deceleration and change of direction"; and "for each case study... the sport-specific skill progressions and how the technical and tactical tasks were integrated" (~00:39-01:17). He also states the cases were deliberately chosen to minimize individual complexity so the framework's application would read clearly, while acknowledging "no case is ever entirely free from complexity" (~01:21-01:45), and that he included cases that "didn't go perfect to show that the real world is not always that way" (~01:45-01:51).

**Why it works** — No stated mechanism; this is a presentation and documentation structure Harries uses for teaching, not a claim about rehab physiology or efficacy.

**When to apply** — As a template for a Baylor RTP case log or after-action review: for a returning athlete, record (1) the RTP timeline/calendar, (2) the loading structure and how it was progressed, (3) max-velocity progression, (4) MDSA progression, and (5) sport-skill progression. Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates "do not yet exist" at Applied Performance and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work; this five-element structure is a ready-made scaffold specifically for RTP case documentation, distinct from that broader reporting gap.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a presentation structure built for four selected, deliberately simplified cases, not a validated clinical documentation standard, and Harries does not claim it captures everything relevant to an actual RTP decision. It has no explicit slot for the competitive-exposure/hesitation criteria in [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] and [[heuristic--hesitation-signals-unready-but-is-unmeasured]] (those show up folded into the sport-skill-progression element in practice, not as their own listed element). Do not treat the five elements as exhaustive without adding Baylor's own required documentation fields (medical clearance sign-off, testing-battery results, incident/mechanism detail) alongside them.

**Example** — Each of the four case-study entries in this folder already follows this five-element order in its own body sections (rehab timeline in "What it is," then loading structure, MV progression, MDSA, sport-specific skill as separate paragraphs), though none names the structure explicitly; see [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] for the clearest example.

# Fitting Rehab Sessions Into the Team's Own Training Week

**What it is** — As a returning athlete moves from an isolated running-only schedule into overlapping with team training, Harries shapes each week of rehab around the team's own weekly training rhythm, not a fixed rehab-only calendar. Case 1, week 3: "a high moderate high structure, including partial training exposure in the midweek, and a heavier modified training session on the weekend" (~05:18-05:27). Case 1, week 4: "one light partial session, a full training midweek, and a walkthrough style session... And then they played their game at the end of the week" (~05:27-05:37). Case 2, week 3: a small on-field rehab session early in the week, a return to partial training midweek, then "a larger combined rehab session with modified team training" at week's end (~17:44-17:56). Case 2, week 4: two non-consecutive training days then two consecutive days, the second-to-last being "a captain's run walkthrough style session, though very low intensity," followed by return to play in a match (~17:56-18:10). Case 4 (knee), week 5: running frequency was deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions "in order to make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions," explicitly to bridge into the larger session planned at the end of week 6 (~37:24-37:46). Case 4, week 7 (the RTP week): "a small session early in the week, a moderate session mid-week, which was aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season," then return to play at week's end (~38:13-38:26).

**Why it works** — For the Case 4 frequency cut, Harries states the reason directly: reducing running frequency let him "make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions" so there was "a nice little progression into" the larger, match-comparable session planned for the following week (~37:26-37:55). For the broader practice of shaping rehab-week structure around the team's rhythm, his only stated reason is the week-7 mid-week session "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (~38:20-38:22); he gives no further explicit rationale for the general practice. Inference (entry writer's): tying rehab-session load to the team's own hard/light day pattern lets the returning athlete's tolerance build in step with what full training will actually demand in the week he returns, rather than on a schedule disconnected from it.

**When to apply** — When designing a returning athlete's week once he is off an isolated running-only schedule and beginning to overlap with team sessions (typically mid-to-late rehab, alongside modified/partial training participation). Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records an existing preference for undulating, not linear, weekly periodization ("waving volume week to week"), and an explicit note that a "training week" does not have to equal 7 calendar days but should be built around the team's real competition schedule; this on-field-rehab pattern applies that same logic to one returning athlete inside the team's actual week.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed template; no claim is made that a "high-moderate-high" week or a captain's-run walkthrough is required, and the specific weekly shapes differ across all three cases that show them, tracking each athlete's own timeline and injury type. None of it is validated against outcome data beyond what happened in each case being reported without a stated recurrence. Do not import a specific case's weekly pattern wholesale as a template; use the underlying idea, build the rehab week around the team's actual week, and rebuild the specific days for each returning athlete.

**Example** — See [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]], weeks 5-7, for the clearest stated rationale: a frequency cut used as a deliberate bridge to a larger session, and an RTP week deliberately matched to the team's normal in-season training rhythm.

# HSR/VHSR Delivery Shifts: Structured Repeats, Then Short Intervals, Then Small-Sided Games

**What it is** — Across the case studies, high-speed running (HSR/VHSR) volume is not just dosed up session to session, it is delivered through three successive formats as rehab advances. Early sessions accumulate HSR through structured, individually-prescribed repeats over a fixed distance (e.g. 100 m and 60 m repeats). From around mid-rehab (session 5 in Case 1, session 3 in Case 2), HSR shifts to short interval formats: "10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, or 15 seconds on and off" (Case 1, ~10:17-10:35), and "short interval, high intensity interval training formats, like 10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, 20 seconds on, 20 seconds off" (Case 2, ~23:14-23:22). From around session 7-8, small-sided games and technical/tactical drills start to contribute HSR/VHSR "a little bit more meaningfully" or "more organically," alongside whatever prescribed running work continues (Case 1, ~10:35-10:46; Case 2, ~23:25-23:30). The same three-stage shift shows up in Case 4, a knee-joint case kept straight-line-only through session 6 for bracing reasons: small-sided games begin contributing to VHSR/sprint load from session 8 (~41:29-41:37).

**Why it works** — Harries does not give an explicit mechanism for why the delivery format itself should shift (his only nearby general statement is that session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding," said of the mid-rehab checkpoint, not this format shift specifically, ~20:08-20:14). Inference (entry writer's): moving from individually-prescribed, fixed-distance repeats to short intervals to game-based drills lets the athlete accumulate the same category of high-speed exposure in progressively less predictable, more sport-representative contexts, without needing to represcribe every rep once basic mechanics and pacing are established.

# The Five-Element Case-Review Structure

**What it is** — Harries reviews each of his four case studies through the same five elements, stated explicitly: "the rehab timeline, which is a high-level overview of the return to play calendar"; "the loading structure. So how was loading planned and how was it progressed across on-field rehab"; "the progression of maximum velocity and how those linear running intensities were increased"; "our multi-directional speed and agility progressions and how we developed acceleration, deceleration and change of direction"; and "for each case study... the sport-specific skill progressions and how the technical and tactical tasks were integrated" (~00:39-01:17). He also states the cases were deliberately chosen to minimize individual complexity so the framework's application would read clearly, while acknowledging "no case is ever entirely free from complexity" (~01:21-01:45), and that he included cases that "didn't go perfect to show that the real world is not always that way" (~01:45-01:51).

**Why it works** — No stated mechanism; this is a presentation and documentation structure Harries uses for teaching, not a claim about rehab physiology or efficacy.

**When to apply** — As a template for a Baylor RTP case log or after-action review: for a returning athlete, record (1) the RTP timeline/calendar, (2) the loading structure and how it was progressed, (3) max-velocity progression, (4) MDSA progression, and (5) sport-skill progression. Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates "do not yet exist" at Applied Performance and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work; this five-element structure is a ready-made scaffold specifically for RTP case documentation, distinct from that broader reporting gap.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a presentation structure built for four selected, deliberately simplified cases, not a validated clinical documentation standard, and Harries does not claim it captures everything relevant to an actual RTP decision. It has no explicit slot for the competitive-exposure/hesitation criteria in [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] and [[heuristic--hesitation-signals-unready-but-is-unmeasured]] (those show up folded into the sport-skill-progression element in practice, not as their own listed element). Do not treat the five elements as exhaustive without adding Baylor's own required documentation fields (medical clearance sign-off, testing-battery results, incident/mechanism detail) alongside them.

**Example** — Each of the four case-study entries in this folder already follows this five-element order in its own body sections (rehab timeline in "What it is," then loading structure, MV progression, MDSA, sport-specific skill as separate paragraphs), though none names the structure explicitly; see [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] for the clearest example.

# HSR/VHSR Delivery Shifts: Structured Repeats, Then Short Intervals, Then Small-Sided Games

**What it is** — Across the case studies, high-speed running (HSR/VHSR) volume is not just dosed up session to session, it is delivered through three successive formats as rehab advances. Early sessions accumulate HSR through structured, individually-prescribed repeats over a fixed distance (e.g. 100 m and 60 m repeats). From around mid-rehab (session 5 in Case 1, session 3 in Case 2), HSR shifts to short interval formats: "10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, or 15 seconds on and off" (Case 1, ~10:17-10:35), and "short interval, high intensity interval training formats, like 10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, 20 seconds on, 20 seconds off" (Case 2, ~23:14-23:22). From around session 7-8, small-sided games and technical/tactical drills start to contribute HSR/VHSR "a little bit more meaningfully" or "more organically," alongside whatever prescribed running work continues (Case 1, ~10:35-10:46; Case 2, ~23:25-23:30). A similar shift to small-sided games shows up in Case 4, a knee-joint case kept straight-line-only through session 6 for bracing reasons: "small-sided games, so modified rehab specific drills and also partial participation with the team" began at session 8 (~41:34-41:40). Harries reports a separate, linear VHSR/sprint increase from sessions 4-8 in the same passage (~41:43-41:46) without explicitly linking the two statements, so this case supports the format shift itself but not a stated causal link to VHSR volume.

**Why it works** — Harries does not give an explicit mechanism for why the delivery format itself should shift (his only nearby general statement is that session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding," said of the mid-rehab checkpoint, not this format shift specifically, ~20:08-20:14). Inference (entry writer's): moving from individually-prescribed, fixed-distance repeats to short intervals to game-based drills lets the athlete accumulate the same category of high-speed exposure in progressively less predictable, more sport-representative contexts, without needing to represcribe every rep once basic mechanics and pacing are established.

**When to apply** — Use as the default organizing structure for programming HSR/VHSR volume across an on-field rehab block, once basic linear mechanics and pacing are established (roughly Level 1-2, see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]). Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that Baylor has no documented phased RTP protocol of its own yet; this three-stage shift is a directly transferable structure to pair with Baylor's own GPS velocity-band thresholds.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed session-count rule; the session numbers cited here (5, 3, 7, 8) are case-specific, not a stated formula, and the source's own repeated caveat is that the framework is a guide adjusted to context, not a step-by-step protocol (see [[principle--framework-is-a-guide-not-a-protocol]]). The Case 4 example also shows the shift can run alongside other, unrelated restrictions (change-of-direction was still withheld through session 6 there for bracing reasons); do not treat "small-sided games by session 7-8" as evidence that all restrictions lift on that same timeline. Do not import a specific case's session numbers as a prescription.

**Example** — In [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]], HSR moved from 100 m repeats (session 2, which overshot the low 17 km/h threshold, see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]) to short intervals (session 3) to small-sided games contributing HSR organically (session 8).

**Related** — [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]; [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]]; [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]; [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]]

# Fitting Rehab Sessions Into the Team's Own Training Week

**What it is** — As a returning athlete moves from an isolated running-only schedule into overlapping with team training, Harries shapes each week of rehab around the team's own weekly training rhythm, not a fixed rehab-only calendar. Case 2: "by week three, we started to fall into the team's training structure a bit more" (~17:40-17:44): a small on-field rehab session early in the week, a return to partial training midweek, then "a larger combined rehab session with modified team training" at week's end (~17:45-17:56). Case 2, week 4: two non-consecutive training days then two consecutive days, the second-to-last being "a captain's run walkthrough style session, though very low intensity," followed by return to play in a match (~17:56-18:10). Case 1, week 3: "a high moderate high structure, including partial training exposure in the midweek, and a heavier modified training session on the weekend" (~05:18-05:27). Case 1, week 4: "one light partial session, a full training midweek, and a walkthrough style session... And then they played their game at the end of the week" (~05:27-05:37). Case 4 (knee), week 5: running frequency was deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions "in order to make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions," explicitly to bridge into the larger session planned at the end of week 6 (~37:24-37:46). Case 4, week 7 (the RTP week): "a small session early in the week, a moderate session mid-week, which was aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season," then return to play at week's end (~38:13-38:26).

**Why it works** — For the Case 4 frequency cut, Harries states the reason directly: reducing running frequency let him "make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions" so there was "a nice little progression into" the larger, match-comparable session planned for the following week (~37:26-37:55). For the broader practice of shaping rehab-week structure around the team's rhythm, his only stated reason is the week-7 mid-week session "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (~38:20-38:22); he gives no further explicit rationale for the general practice. Inference (entry writer's): tying rehab-session load to the team's own hard/light day pattern lets the returning athlete's tolerance build in step with what full training will actually demand in the week he returns, rather than on a schedule disconnected from it.

**When to apply** — When designing a returning athlete's week once he is off an isolated running-only schedule and beginning to overlap with team sessions (typically mid-to-late rehab, alongside modified/partial training participation). Eric's review: Applied Performance "already undulate[s] load across the team week," and this pattern is proposed as "the same logic applied to one returning player, anchored to the team's Tue/Wed high, Thu low pattern" (Review and Plan, line 75) - i.e. the existing team-week undulation is the natural anchor for this on-field-rehab pattern, not a separate structure to invent.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed template; no claim is made that a "high-moderate-high" week or a captain's-run walkthrough is required, and the specific weekly shapes differ across all three cases that show them, tracking each athlete's own timeline and injury type. None of it is validated against outcome data beyond what happened in each case being reported without a stated recurrence. # HSR/VHSR Delivery Shifts: Structured Repeats, Then Short Intervals, Then Small-Sided Games

**What it is** — Across the case studies, high-speed running (HSR/VHSR) volume is not just dosed up session to session, it is delivered through three successive formats as rehab advances. Early sessions accumulate HSR through structured, individually-prescribed repeats over a fixed distance (e.g. 100 m and 60 m repeats). From around mid-rehab (session 5 in Case 1, session 3 in Case 2), HSR shifts to short interval formats: "10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, or 15 seconds on and off" (Case 1, ~10:17-10:35), and "short interval, high intensity interval training formats, like 10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, 20 seconds on, 20 seconds off" (Case 2, ~23:14-23:22). From around session 7-8, small-sided games and technical/tactical drills start to contribute HSR/VHSR "a little bit more meaningfully" or "more organically," alongside whatever prescribed running work continues (Case 1, ~10:35-10:46; Case 2, ~23:25-23:30). A similar shift to small-sided games shows up in Case 4, a knee-joint case kept straight-line-only through session 6 for bracing reasons: "small-sided games, so modified rehab specific drills and also partial participation with the team" began at session 8 (~41:34-41:40). Harries reports a separate, linear VHSR/sprint increase from sessions 4-8 in the same passage (~41:43-41:46) without explicitly linking the two statements, so this case supports the format shift itself but not a stated causal link to VHSR volume.

**Why it works** — Harries does not give an explicit mechanism for why the delivery format itself should shift (his only nearby general statement is that session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding," said of the mid-rehab checkpoint, not this format shift specifically, ~20:08-20:14). Inference (entry writer's): moving from individually-prescribed, fixed-distance repeats to short intervals to game-based drills lets the athlete accumulate the same category of high-speed exposure in progressively less predictable, more sport-representative contexts, without needing to represcribe every rep once basic mechanics and pacing are established.

**When to apply** — Use as the default organizing structure for programming HSR/VHSR volume across an on-field rehab block, once basic linear mechanics and pacing are established (roughly Level 1-2, see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]). Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that Baylor has no documented phased RTP protocol of its own yet; this three-stage shift is a directly transferable structure to pair with Baylor's own GPS velocity-band thresholds.

# Fitting Rehab Sessions Into the Team's Own Training Week

**What it is** — As a returning athlete moves from an isolated running-only schedule into overlapping with team training, Harries shapes each week of rehab around the team's own weekly training rhythm, not a fixed rehab-only calendar. Case 2: "by week three, we started to fall into the team's training structure a bit more" (~17:40-17:44): a small on-field rehab session early in the week, a return to partial training midweek, then "a larger combined rehab session with modified team training" at week's end (~17:45-17:56). Case 2, week 4: two non-consecutive training days then two consecutive days, the second-to-last being "a captain's run walkthrough style session, though very low intensity," followed by return to play in a match (~17:56-18:10). Case 1, week 3: "a high moderate high structure, including partial training exposure in the midweek, and a heavier modified training session on the weekend" (~05:18-05:27). Case 1, week 4: "one light partial session, a full training midweek, and a walkthrough style session... And then they played their game at the end of the week" (~05:27-05:37). Case 4 (knee), week 5: running frequency was deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions "in order to make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions," explicitly to bridge into the larger session planned at the end of week 6 (~37:24-37:46). Case 4, week 7 (the RTP week): "a small session early in the week, a moderate session mid-week, which was aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season," then return to play at week's end (~38:13-38:26).

For the broader practice of shaping rehab-week structure around the team's rhythm, his only stated reason is the week-7 mid-week session "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (~38:20-38:22); he gives no further explicit rationale for the general practice. Inference (entry writer's): tying rehab-session load to the team's own hard/light day pattern lets the returning athlete's tolerance build in step with what full training will actually demand in the week he returns, rather than on a schedule disconnected from it.
